title: Year two close: the whole Torah
hook: the whole Torah, the whole prayer book, the whole year, now known from the inside
carry: the torah, the prayer, the year

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu B'Av, white dresses in the vineyards. Your line was after mourning, love. Today, the last day of year two.

Five times a year, something special happens in synagogue. The reader reaches the last verse of one of the Torah's five books. In some congregations everyone rises, and the whole room calls out three words: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened. Not well done. Be strong. This year's lessons reached that shout four times: at the end of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Today it comes once more, at the end of the whole year.
screen: `THE LAST VERSE OF A BOOK.` → `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.` → `FOUR BOOKS THIS YEAR.`

segments.voice: Year two began in the middle of the plagues and walked the people out of Egypt, through the sea, to Sinai, and into a tent of meeting built from everyone's gifts. Then Leviticus, the book of holiness, with its offerings and its sudden line, in the old Jewish translation: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Then Numbers: forty years of wilderness, complaints, manna and a donkey that talked. Then Deuteronomy, Moses' long goodbye, ending on Mount Nebo with a land he could see and not enter, and a grave no one knows. On Simchat Torah the scroll rolled straight back to the beginning. Then the prayer book, in order: thanking God on waking for the rooster's sense to tell day from night; the Shema, a hand over the eyes; the Amidah, feet together, three steps in; Shabbat, and the quiet personal prayers at the end. Then the year: the Days of Awe, the sukkah, winter's lights, Purim's noise, the Passover table, forty-nine days of counting, Sinai as a wedding, Ruth choosing to stay, and this summer's walls, floor and vineyards. Three circles, each one turning. The Torah is read through every year and begins again the moment it ends. The prayers come back three times a day. The year comes back every year. None is ever finished; that's the point. So the words at the end of a book don't say you made it. They say be strong, and the plural is the key: let us be strengthened, together. A people that keeps the same scroll, prayers and days holds each other up by doing it.
screen: `EXODUS TO DEUTERONOMY.` · `THE PRAYER BOOK, PAGE BY PAGE.` · `THE YEAR, FEAST AND FAST.` · `THREE CIRCLES, NEVER FINISHED.` · then, large: `THE TORAH, THE PRAYER, THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Let a few of this year's blessings pass by: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure; the one thanking God for strength to the weary; blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. If you pray, say one slowly, in Hebrew or English; if not, say quietly the one line from this year that stayed with you.
Chazak. Be strong: the shout at the end of each book of the Torah, and the word that closes the whole year, each circle beginning again.
Your line: the torah, the prayer, the year. Be strong, and let us be strengthened. Year two, complete.

howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in the synagogue, the congregation, often standing, calls out "chazak, chazak, venitchazek" (be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened), and the reader repeats it.

chat.says: Why does everyone call out 'be strong' when a book of the Torah ends?
options: The reading never finishes; it starts again, and people strengthen each other.
It congratulates the reader for getting through a book without mistakes.
It warns that the next book of the Torah is harder to read aloud.
chat.meaning: The circles never finish, so the words say chazak, chazak, venitchazek: be strong, and let us be strengthened, together.

notes: Chazak custom: Ashkenazi congregations call 'chazak, chazak, venitchazek' at the end of each book; Sephardi custom differs (often 'chazak u'baruch' to the reader). The script says 'in many congregations'; a Keeper may want to name the variation.
Standing for the end of a book is a widespread but not universal custom.
The link of chazak to Moses' charge to Joshua (Deut 31:7, Joshua 1) is a common explanation; verify phrasing in the trapdoor.
Year-two look-back summarizes Blocks A–F of y2.md; check that the named items (talking donkey, rooster blessing, three steps, Sinai as a wedding, Ruth) match earlier days.
Blessings in the practice are described in English paraphrase, not quoted from a translation; no new prayer is written.
'Five times a year': once per book in the annual cycle; Simchat Torah completes Deuteronomy.
